1.pericope_label: Certain women which ministered unto him of their substance

schools.summary: Say more briefly that it has been commonly supposed and that there is not the least evidence for it, and take seven for an indefinite number signifying a grievous torment. Or supply the material the tradition feeds on, reporting a Talmudic Maria Magdila who was an adulteress and a town near Jerusalem of very ill fame, so that she might be called Magdalene either from living there or from imitating its customs; and derive Chuza from Haman's genealogy, concluding it an Idumean name fitting for a man in the household of Herod, who was of the blood of the Edomites. Give the seven devils a clinical sense instead, of a specially aggravated possession with paroxysms of delirious frenzy like those of the Gadarene. And picture two travelling companies, the Master and the Twelve heralding his approach in synagogue or market-place or open plain, and a separate company of devout women, mostly of the wealthier class, journeying probably in advance to arrange for his reception and food, since it was said to be no uncommon practice for women of independent means to support a teacher in his work.

Turn their history into an argument about grace: to be attended by women marked with infamy might be thought dishonourable to the Son of God, but the crimes with which we were loaded before we believed do not diminish his glory, since it is not said that the Church he elected was found without spot but that he cleansed it; they were pointed at with the finger on every side, and willingly endured to have their shame made known provided the grace of Christ were not concealed. Alongside this, contest the Idumean derivation of the steward's name on the manuscripts, since in one edition of that treatise Haman's ancestor is not Chuza but Ciza, and Chuza is a Jewish name borne by a family of note.

Protest against the tradition. Commentators have a marvellous propensity to make the women of the Sacred Writings appear women of ill fame, so that one must be a harlot and this one a prostitute, though nothing of the kind can be proved in either case; she is presented simply as one who had been possessed with seven demons, among other women healed of evil spirits and infirmities, and the other two named might as well come in for a share of the censure. Add a prudential argument: had she been such, the world that knew her character could not see the inward change, and Christ's enemies, ready enough to call him the friend of publicans and sinners, would have seized so favourable an opportunity, yet they never said he was the friend of prostitutes. Conclude that the common opinion is a vile slander on one of the best women in the Gospel, and complain that houses for the reception of such bear her name. Take the seven for a superlative rather than a count.

Find the whole arrangement prophesied, applying to these wealthy ladies the summons to the women that are at ease to rise up and hear, so that they were proved first as disciples and then as helpers, following in labour and ministering with hope. Or describe the method rather than the company: like the eagle enticing its young to fly, our Lord raises his disciples step by step, teaching first in the synagogues, then choosing the twelve, then taking them with him through the cities and villages.

debates.question: Was Mary Magdalene a woman of ill fame?

sides.position: No, and the common opinion is a vile slander — Christ's enemies would have used it against him had it been true
No — it has been commonly supposed, but there is not the least evidence for it
There is material for it: a Talmudic Maria Magdila who was an adulteress, and a town of ill fame whose customs she may have imitated
She is distinguished from the rest, who were matrons of spotless reputation cured of ordinary diseases, as one in whom Christ gave a signal display of his power

debates.question: Is Chuza an Idumean name or a Jewish one?

sides.position: Idumean — the name occurs in Haman's genealogy, and fits a man in the household of Herod, who was of Edomite blood
Jewish — the genealogy reads Ciza in one edition, and Chuza is the name of a family of note among the Jews

outliers.note: Alone turns the question into an argument from the silence of Christ's enemies, since they called him the friend of publicans and sinners but never the friend of prostitutes, which they would have done had a converted one ministered to him.
Alone treats the women's ministry as fulfilled prophecy, applying to them the summons to the women at ease to rise up and hear, so that they were proved first as disciples and then as helpers.
Alone reconstructs the logistics, describing two companies on the road, the Twelve heralding the approach and the women travelling in advance to arrange the reception and the food.

themes: And it came to pass afterward, that he went throughout every city and village, preaching and shewing the glad tidings of the kingdom of God: and the twelve were with him,
And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils,
And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod’s steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance.

4.pericope_label: A sower went out to sow his seed

schools.summary: List what is added here and nowhere else: his seed, the trampling under foot, the birds of the heavens, and the word for moisture, which occurs in the New Testament only in this verse. Press the same words for their sense, preferring upon the rock to the stony or rocky ground of the other two reports as the more accurate term, and take the statement that it withered because it lacked moisture to be not without its force in the spiritual interpretation, the moisture being the dew and rain of God's grace, without which the seed could not put forth its roots; so that the two failures on the rock are distinct, the lack of moisture representing one aspect of what was wanting and the having no depth of earth another.

Hold that Christ is chiefly designed by the sower, since the phrase his seed, which only this evangelist has, best agrees with him, he being both the proprietor and the subject of it, though it is true of every preacher of the gospel; and take the ground chosen to be first the people of the Jews and afterwards the Gentiles. On the rock, identify the hearers whose hearts are hardened through the deceitfulness of sin and continue so notwithstanding the preaching of the word.

Take no interest in the concealment and dwell on the concourse: they came out of every city and would not stay till he came to them, meeting him when he was coming toward them and following him when he was going from them; nor would he excuse himself from going to the cities on that account, for he is found of those that sought him not.

Give two reasons for the veil that pull opposite ways: the Lord speaks by a parable first that he may make his hearers more attentive, since men were accustomed to exercise their minds on dark sayings and to despise what was plain, and next that the unworthy might not receive what was spoken mystically; and find the method foretold in the psalm that promises to open the mouth in parables. Or divide the hearers before the parable divides them, into those made worthy of the heavenly calling who fall from grace through carelessness and sloth, and those who multiply the seed; note that the other evangelist makes three divisions within each class, since those who corrupt the seed have not all the same manner of destruction; and explain the loss on the wayside without any fault in the hearer, since some, though they have not sinned, have lost the good seed through its being withdrawn from their thoughts by evil spirits, or by deceitful and cunning men, whom he calls the birds of the air.

Read the crowd against the parable: much people were gathered together and were come out of every city, and yet not many but few there are who walk the strait road and find the way that leads to life; hence the other evangelist says that he taught without the house by parables, but within the house explained the parable to his disciples.

debates.question: Why did he teach the multitude in parables?

sides.position: Both to attract and to exclude — to make the hearers more attentive, since men exercise their minds on dark sayings, and that the unworthy might not receive what was spoken mystically
Because few walk the strait road: he taught without the house by parables and explained within the house to his disciples

debates.question: What is lost when the seed falls by the wayside?

sides.position: Something lost without any fault in the hearer: some who have not sinned lose the seed by its being withdrawn from their thoughts by evil spirits or by cunning men
Something lost through hardness: hearers whose hearts are hardened by the deceitfulness of sin and continue so under the preaching

outliers.note: Alone sorts the hearers into two classes and then three subdivisions within each before the parable is interpreted, and alone excuses the wayside hearers of any sin in the loss of the seed.
Alone gives the lack of moisture a spiritual force distinct from the want of depth, making it the dew and rain of God's grace without which the seed cannot root.
Alone answers the concourse with the observation that Christ would not excuse himself from going to the cities because some had come out of them, for he is found of those that sought him not.

themes: And when much people were gathered together, and were come to him out of every city, he spake by a parable:
A sower went out to sow his seed: and as he sowed, some fell by the way side; and it was trodden down, and the fowls of the air devoured it.
And some fell upon a rock; and as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it lacked moisture.
And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.
And other fell on good ground, and sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold. And when he had said these things, he cried, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.

9.pericope_label: The seed is the word of God: what the four grounds are

schools.summary: Report the grammatical difficulty, that one evangelist uses a particle of purpose here where another uses one of cause, and pass on the resolution that there is truth in both: Jesus speaks in parables because the multitudes see without seeing and hear without hearing, and also in order that they may. Note that the prophet's words are given here without being quoted as such. On the interpretation, observe that the phrase the word of God, which stands here for the word of the kingdom in the other report, is a favourite of this evangelist and rare elsewhere, and that with the article on both sides the terms are interchangeable, so the word of God is the seed; add that it is to be taken in its widest sense, as including every form by which a revelation from God reaches the mind of man. Note that the devil is named here where the others say Satan or the wicked one, and that the purpose given is fuller, lest they should believe and be saved, which is the plain reason why preaching fails. On the good ground, explain that one word means really good or generous and the other beautiful or noble, that the Greeks joined them to describe the high-minded gentleman, and that the pair occurs here alone in the New Testament, though the evangelist adds moral qualities the pagan phrase did not carry; and prefer perseverance to patience, since the word implies something more vigorous than passive submission, and there is no other way for real fruit to come, mushrooms springing up overnight while the best fruits require time and cultivation.

Insist on perseverance rather than patience, since good ground continues to bear because it is strong and vigorous, and poor ground is soon exhausted; from which draw that the perseverance of the saints necessarily implies continuing to bring forth fruit, and that those who are not fruitful are not in a state of perseverance.

Turn the whole into a privilege to be felt rather than a problem to be solved: those who would receive instruction from Christ must consider what a distinguishing privilege it is to be led into the light when others are left in darkness, and how happy we are if what is a parable to others, with which they are only amused, is a plain truth to us.

Report the objection as a dispute, where one party asks what sort of God causes blindness and the other answers from the apostle that the gospel is veiled only in them that are perishing, since it is not right to give holy things to dogs; and apply that to this verse, asking whether the Lord wished them not to see from hatred, or because of their unworthiness, since they had closed their own eyes, for where there is wilful wickedness there is also a withholding of grace.

debates.question: Were the parables meant to conceal, or did they only happen to conceal?

sides.position: Both, and the grammar of the two Gospels carries both: he speaks in parables because they see without seeing, and in order that they may
Because of their unworthiness, not from hatred: they had closed their own eyes, and where there is wilful wickedness there is a withholding of grace
The question is not to be solved but felt, as the privilege of being led into the light while others are left in darkness

debates.question: Is the last word of the parable patience or perseverance?

sides.position: Perseverance, and it proves a doctrine: those who are not fruitful are not in a state of perseverance
Perseverance or steadfastness, as something more vigorous than the passive submission we associate with patience

outliers.note: Alone brings a set debate to the verse, in which one party asks what sort of God causes blindness and the other answers that the gospel is veiled only in them that are perishing.

Alone answers the difficulty by refusing to choose between the causal and the final reading, and alone illustrates the last clause by observing that mushrooms spring up overnight while the best fruits require time and cultivation.
Alone turns the word for patience into a test of the perseverance of the saints, arguing that it necessarily implies continuing to bring forth fruit.

themes: And his disciples asked him, saying, What might this parable be?
And he said, Unto you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God: but to others in parables; that seeing they might not see, and hearing they might not understand.
Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.
Those by the way side are they that hear; then cometh the devil, and taketh away the word out of their hearts, lest they should believe and be saved.
They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.
And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection.
But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.

16.pericope_label: No man lighteth a candle and covereth it; and who are my mother and my brethren

schools.summary: Prefer lamp to candle and lampstand to candlestick, note the general word vessel where the others have the bushel, and mark the wider range of the light, which reaches not only those in the house but those entering it; venture to connect that with the evangelist's own history as a convert from heathenism, who had been among those that entered in and had seen the light the apostles lighted. Answer the inference drawn from another evangelist's distributing these sayings over three separate places: it does not follow that anyone has bunched separate sayings together or scattered a single discourse, since one of the slowest lessons for some critics to learn is that Jesus repeated favourite sayings on different occasions, as every popular preacher does. On the closing proverb, keep the appearance and make it the point: better, that which he thinks he hath, since the man who does not use his knowledge has no real possession in it.

Defend the visitors' motive against two of the fathers by name, allowing that natural affection may have carried them beyond the bounds of propriety but refusing the charge of ambition, since the testimony of the Spirit everywhere commends Mary's piety and modesty.

Argue that the common rendering, what he seemeth to have, contradicts itself, since what is possessed in appearance only can be taken away in appearance only, so that there is neither gain nor loss and the text says nothing; show from classical usage that the verb is often an expletive or an intensive, and conclude it means simply what he hath, these persons having really had the divine seed planted in them.

Apply the lamp to the disciples, teaching them to be strong as exposed to the view of all men, fighting in the world as on a stage, since so great virtue cannot lie hid. On the mother and the brethren, deny that the answer reproves Mary, holding that it greatly assists her, since he would not have raised her so high if she were always to expect honour from him as a son and never to consider him as her Lord. Or report a reading in which the message is malicious, brought by men who mocked his teaching and meant to expose his meanness of birth, and answer that low birth harms no one who hears the word of God, though hearing alone saves none and rather condemns. Or take the word brethren as a doctrine of grace, since no one is the brother of the Saviour in respect of his divine nature, he being the Only-begotten, but he has made us partakers of his flesh and blood and, being God by nature, has become our brother.

Make the candlestick the whole Church, and say that he who lights the light of reason in his soul must not hide it under a bed where men sleep, since that provides nothing for those entering the house.

Read the lamp as the sequel to the privilege just given, that having told the apostles the mysteries were for them and parables for others, the Lord now shows that by them the same mystery must at length be revealed to others. Or read the covering as cowardice rather than reticence, taking the vessel and bed for the flesh and the lamp for the word, so that whoever keeps it hid through fear of the troubles of the flesh sets the flesh before the manifestation of the truth; and set against him the man who so submits his body to God's service that preaching the truth stands highest and the service of the body lowest.

debates.question: Does 'that which he seemeth to have' mean an appearance or a possession?

sides.position: A possession: the common rendering contradicts itself, since what is held in appearance can be lost only in appearance, and the verb is often merely intensive
An appearance, and that is the point: what he thinks he hath, since the man who does not use his knowledge has no real possession in it

debates.question: What does the answer about his mother and brethren do to Mary?

sides.position: It assists her rather than reproves her, since he would not have raised her so high if she were never to consider him as her Lord
It answers a malicious message meant to expose his meanness of birth, and shows that low birth harms no one who hears the word of God
It leaves her motive untouched: the charge of ambition brought by two of the fathers is without probability, the Spirit everywhere commending her piety and modesty

outliers.note: Alone reads the covering of the lamp as cowardice rather than reticence, making the vessel and the bed the flesh, so that the man who hides the word out of fear sets his body before the manifestation of the truth.
Alone connects the lamp's reach to those entering the house with the evangelist's own history as a convert from heathenism, who had been among those that entered in.

Alone turns the word brethren into a doctrine of the incarnation, since no one is the Saviour's brother by his divine nature, but he who is God by nature has made us partakers of his flesh and blood and become our brother.

themes: No man, when he hath lighted a candle, covereth it with a vessel, or putteth it under a bed; but setteth it on a candlestick, that they which enter in may see the light.
For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.
Take heed therefore how ye hear: for whosoever hath, to him shall be given; and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have.
Then came to him his mother and his brethren, and could not come at him for the press.
And it was told him by certain which said, Thy mother and thy brethren stand without, desiring to see thee.
And he answered and said unto them, My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it.

22.pericope_label: He rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: what manner of man is this

schools.summary: Note that the word for falling asleep differs from the was asleep of the other Gospels and occurs in the New Testament only here, a more technical term and so far characteristic of the physician-historian; that they were filling rather than were filled, the tense describing the process; and that the word rendered Master is one this evangelist alone uses, the more classical of the two, reserving the ordinary word for the Lord's work as a teacher. Observe too that this writer uses the accurate term lake throughout where the other three, written by or under the influence of Galileans, keep the popular sea. Supply the geography, that these wind storms rushed from the mountain down through the gorge upon the small lake and shook it like a tempest, and note that this is the only passage which speaks of the sleep of Jesus; find the disciples' uneasiness in the doubled address, and note that the word for the raging of the water is a boisterous surge rather than the regular swell of the other account.

Work on one English word instead, comparing the phrase for being in jeopardy with the Greek version of the prophet's storm, where the same verb is used of a ship in the utmost danger of being dashed to pieces; and object that jeopardy is an inexpressive borrowed term, properly the cry of a disappointed gamester that the game is lost.

Give the reason from the errand: Christ chose to go by water though he might have gone by land a little way about, that he might show his wonders in the deep; and guess that the prince of the power of the air, suspecting Christ was crossing to cast out the legion on the other side, poured out this storm to stop him.

Explain why they were put out on the water at all: the disciples had seen all men receive help from Christ, and it seemed fitting that they too should have the benefit of him, since no one regards what happens to another equally with what happens to himself; so the Lord exposed them to the sea and the winds.

Read the crossing as the type of every Christian passage: no one can pass from this life without temptations, temptation being the trial of faith, so we are subject to the storms of spiritual wickedness and must awake the Pilot as watchful sailors; and though Christ no longer sleeps in the sleep of his own body, beware lest through the sleep of our bodies he be to us asleep. Be sharpest on the rebuke that follows: they are rightly reproved who feared while Christ was present, since he who clings to him can in no wise perish. Or settle the difficulty of the three different cries, since it is not worth while to inquire which was most likely said, whether they said one of these three or some other of the same import being no matter; and among the many who awoke him all these things may have been said, one by one and another by another. Or use the miracle against an opponent by name, since to ask what manner of man commands the winds and water is not to find a new proprietor of the elements: the rod of Moses waved over a sea ampler than all the lakes of that country, the Jordan stood still at the bidding of Joshua's priests, and the psalm had already said that the Lord is upon many waters.

debates.question: Why were the disciples brought into the storm?

sides.position: That they might have the benefit of Christ in their own persons, since no one regards what happens to another equally with what happens to himself
Because temptation is the trial of faith, and no one passes through this life without it
Because Christ chose the water to show his wonders in the deep — and perhaps because the prince of the power of the air raised the storm to stop the crossing

debates.question: Do the three different forms of the disciples' cry need to be reconciled?

sides.position: No — it is not worth while to inquire which was said, and among the many who woke him all may have been said, one by one and another by another
The doubling of the address in this account is itself the point, showing the disciples' uneasiness

outliers.note: Alone answers the question what manner of man this is by producing the Creator's own credentials, the rod of Moses over the Red Sea, the Jordan halted for Joshua's priests, and the psalm that set the Lord upon many waters.
Alone attacks the English word jeopardy as an inexpressive borrowing, properly the cry of a disappointed gamester that the game is lost, while matching the Greek verb to the storm of the prophet.

Alone builds a portrait of the writer out of his vocabulary, taking the technical word for falling asleep as the physician's and the accurate term lake, against the popular sea of the other three, as the stranger's.

themes: Now it came to pass on a certain day, that he went into a ship with his disciples: and he said unto them, Let us go over unto the other side of the lake. And they launched forth.
But as they sailed he fell asleep: and there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy.
And they came to him, and awoke him, saying, Master, master, we perish. Then he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm.
And he said unto them, Where is your faith? And they being afraid wondered, saying one to another, What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him.

26.pericope_label: The Gadarene delivered from the legion, and sent home to shew what God had done

schools.summary: Resolve the name of the place: the reading here agrees with the second Gospel while the other name belongs to the first, and the discrepancy is cleared up by the discovery of a village of the right name on the steep eastern bank, near the town the other reading points to. Give the word for the deep as well, from a privative and the word for deep, used of the deep sea, of the receptacle of the dead, and especially of the abode of demons.

Decline the smaller question, whether the man was a citizen or came out of the town to meet Christ, observing that when he was sent home he proclaimed the thing in a neighbouring country, from which it is conjectured he was not a native. Refuse three current explanations of the tombs as idle and foolish — that devils delight in the stench of dead bodies, are gratified by the smell of oblations, or watch over souls desirous to approach their bodies — and give another: the man was kept among the graves that he might be terrified continually with the mournful spectacle of death, as if cut off from the society of men and already dwelling among the dead; from which draw that the devil does not only torment men in the present life but pursues them even to death, and that in death his dominion is chiefly exercised. Set the two responses to the miracle side by side: how wide is the difference between the knowledge that strikes men with terror and drives them from the presence of God, and the knowledge that draws them gently and makes them feel that nothing is more desirable than to be united to him.

Report the three forms of the place-name without deciding. Supply a parallel from outside Scripture for the request not to be sent into the deep, that in one school of philosophy certain material demons were said to wander the earth in horror of being sent into abysses, so that if even an old woman threatened them and pronounced the names of the angels whose office that is, their fear would be inexpressible. Then refuse the rationalising reading outright: some critics would have us understand the whole of the man himself, an outrageous maniac who ran after the swine and drove them down the precipice; this is solemn trifling indeed, or at least trifling with solemn things, and it is impossible to read the account as given here and admit that explanation, for on such a plan there is nothing certain in the word of God and every man may give it what meaning he pleases.

Follow the herdsmen: they fled lest they should perish with the swine, and the severity of their loss led them to the Saviour, so that while God punishes men in their substance he confers a blessing on their souls; the healed man sat at the feet where he had obtained safety and departed not from them, while the countrymen, who ought to have besought the Lord to stay and guard them, through fear lost their own salvation by asking him to depart.

Read the scene as a figure of the nations. The brazen fetters signify the harsh and severe laws of the Gentiles, by which offences are restrained in their states; the bursting of them and the driving into the wilderness means that he broke through those laws and was led by lust into crimes beyond the ordinary life of men; the legion signifies the nations that served many devils; and the swine on the mountains are the unclean and proud over whom the evil spirits have dominion because of their idols, men who after the manner of unclean animals have defiled the grace of their natural virtues by the filthy actions of their life.

sides.position: The devils, as the text says — the reading that makes it the maniac himself running after them is solemn trifling, and leaves nothing certain in the word of God
The evil spirits, read as a figure: the swine are the unclean and proud over whom they have dominion because of idolatry

debates.question: Why did the man live among the tombs?

sides.position: For none of the reasons commonly given — that devils delight in the stench of bodies, or the smell of oblations, or watch over souls — but that he might be terrified continually with the spectacle of death
The question is one of place and text rather than motive: the country is the one the manuscripts dispute, now identified on the steep eastern bank

outliers.note: Alone brings in the material demons of one school of philosophy, who are said to dread the abysses so much that a threat from an old woman naming the angels whose office it is would terrify them into flight.

Alone follows the herdsmen and their neighbours through the whole episode, observing that God punishes men in their substance while blessing their souls, and that the countrymen lost their salvation by asking the Lord to depart.
Alone names and rejects three received explanations of the demoniac's dwelling among the graves before offering his own, that the tombs kept the spectacle of death continually before him.

themes: And they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is over against Galilee.
And when he went forth to land, there met him out of the city a certain man, which had devils long time, and ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs.
When he saw Jesus, he cried out, and fell down before him, and with a loud voice said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God most high? I beseech thee, torment me not.

(For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. For oftentimes it had caught him: and he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands, and was driven of the devil into the wilderness.)
And Jesus asked him, saying, What is thy name? And he said, Legion: because many devils were entered into him.
And they besought him that he would not command them to go out into the deep.
And there was there an herd of many swine feeding on the mountain: and they besought him that he would suffer them to enter into them. And he suffered them.
Then went the devils out of the man, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked.
When they that fed them saw what was done, they fled, and went and told it in the city and in the country.

Then they went out to see what was done; and came to Jesus, and found the man, out of whom the devils were departed, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
They also which saw it told them by what means he that was possessed of the devils was healed.
Then the whole multitude of the country of the Gadarenes round about besought him to depart from them; for they were taken with great fear: and he went up into the ship, and returned back again.
Now the man out of whom the devils were departed besought him that he might be with him: but Jesus sent him away, saying,
Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee. And he went his way, and published throughout the whole city how great things Jesus had done unto him.

40.pericope_label: Who touched me? Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole

schools.summary: Note that the words for the crowd's pressure mean to hold thee in and to crush thee, the second used elsewhere of pressing out grapes and occurring in the New Testament only here; and that the title the disciples use in reply is the distinctive word this evangelist alone employs, the same he had used in the storm.

State the objection to the question who touched me: it does appear absurd that Christ should pour out his grace without knowing on whom he bestowed it, and no easier to suppose the power flowed from him unbidden, as though it were not a free gift given at the times and to the persons he was pleased to select. Answer that beyond all question he knowingly and willingly cured the woman, and drew her to himself by his Spirit that she might obtain the cure, but put the question to her so that she might freely and publicly make it known; for if Christ had been the only witness of his own miracle his statements might not have been believed, whereas now that the woman, struck with dread, relates what happened to her, greater weight is due to her confession. Or give the same reason in a sentence, that he spoke not as ignorant of the person but in order to discover her to the people, and the cure she had received, and her faith along with it.

Turn the episode into a rule about faith. The power that went out of him did not proceed always as necessarily as odours do from plants, for then all who touched him must have been equally partakers; of the many that touched him this woman alone received it, because she came in faith, which alone attracts and receives the energetic influence of God at all times. From which draw the complaint that there would be more miracles, at least of spiritual healing, were there more faith among those who are called believers.

Begin from the contrast with the shore just left. Christ was driven away by the Gadarenes, who were weary of him and willing to be rid of him; but when he crossed the water the Galileans gladly received him, having wished and waited for his return, so that if some will not accept the favours he offers, others will, and if one town be not gathered there are many among whom he shall be glorious. Note too that having finished his work on the far side he came back and found fresh work waiting, since they that lay out themselves to do good shall never want occasion for it. On the ruler's approach weigh the manner: the address was humble and reverent, for Jairus, though a ruler, fell down at Jesus' feet as owning him a ruler above himself, and importunate, since he besought him to come into his house, not having the faith, or at least not the thought, of the centurion who desired Christ only to speak the word at a distance; and yet Christ complied and went with him.

Report what became of the woman afterwards, that in the city she came from she set up a monument of the mercy shown her: on a lofty pedestal near the entrance to her house stood a brazen statue of a woman on bended knees with her hands joined as if in prayer, and opposite it another figure of the same material, clothed in a stole and holding forth his hand to her, at whose feet a strange plant was growing up to the hem of the brazen robe.

debates.question: Why did Christ ask who touched him?

sides.position: So that the woman might publish it herself, since if Christ were the only witness of his own miracle his statements might not be believed
To make the point that faith, not contact, drew the power — of the many that touched him this woman alone received it

debates.question: What distinguishes this woman from the crowd that pressed him?

sides.position: Faith alone, which attracts and receives the energetic influence of God at all times
The vocabulary itself marks the difference, the crowd holding him in and crushing him where she merely touched

outliers.note: Alone follows the woman out of the Gospel and into her own city, describing the bronze group she is said to have set up at her door, with the strange plant growing at the feet of the standing figure.

Alone denies that the healing power went out of Christ as odours go from plants, and turns the denial into a complaint that there would be more miracles of spiritual healing were there more faith among those called believers.
Alone sets the welcome of the Galileans against the dismissal by the Gadarenes, drawing the rule that if some will not accept the favours Christ offers, others will.

themes: And it came to pass, that, when Jesus was returned, the people gladly received him: for they were all waiting for him.
And, behold, there came a man named Jairus, and he was a ruler of the synagogue: and he fell down at Jesus’ feet, and besought him that he would come into his house:
For he had one only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she lay a dying. But as he went the people thronged him.
And a woman having an issue of blood twelve years, which had spent all her living upon physicians, neither could be healed of any,
Came behind him, and touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched.
And Jesus said, Who touched me? When all denied, Peter and they that were with him said, Master, the multitude throng thee and press thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?
And Jesus said, Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me.

And when the woman saw that she was not hid, she came trembling, and falling down before him, she declared unto him before all the people for what cause she had touched him, and how she was healed immediately.
And he said unto her, Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.

49.pericope_label: Weep not; she is not dead, but sleepeth

schools.summary: Meet the question whether the child was really dead. Some think the saying about sleep proves she was not dead but only in a trance; it matters little, since the touch of Christ's hand and the power of his voice restored her to life, and the calling aloud was certainly not to wake the dead but to make it plain to all that she rose in answer to his raised voice. Note also that this account agrees with the second Gospel in naming the three who were allowed in, where the first omits them.

Give the mourners evidential weight, since the evangelists mention the lamentation so that the resurrection may be more fully believed, hired mourners not being present until the death had been ascertained and the funeral preparations were going forward. But do not let the custom pass without a rebuke: it was their duty to employ every method for allaying grief, and instead, as though they had not sinned enough in disorderly lamentation, they were eager to heighten it by fresh excitements, which shows how strongly inclined the world is not only to indulge its faults but to promote them. Alongside this, take the return of her spirit as doctrine, that the soul is immortal and dies not with the body, existing in a separate state after death and hereafter re-entering the body in the resurrection, of which this was a kind of pledge and emblem; and decline to ask where her spirit was during the separation, calling the question needless, and it enough to say that it had returned to God who gave it.

Say of the funeral practice in one line that pompous ceremonies are ridiculous in themselves and entirely opposed to the spirit and simplicity of the religion of Christ. Then draw the largest lesson from the smallest detail, the command to give her something to eat: though she was raised by a miracle she was not to be preserved by one, since nature is God's great instrument and he delights to work by it, nor will he do anything by his sovereign power in the way of miracle that can be effected by his ordinary providence; and press the parallel, that God will have us be workers together with him, providing food but not eating for us, and providing salvation for a lost world and bestowing it on every penitent believing soul, yet neither repenting nor believing for any man.

Explain the delay as design: the Lord conveniently waited until the girl had died, so that the miracle of her raising might be made public, and for that reason he goes slower and speaks longer with the woman, that the ruler's daughter may expire and the messengers come to tell him.

Read the taking of the hand as the figure of a greater feeding, calling him blessed whom wisdom takes by the hand to bring him into her secret places and command that food be given him, since the bread of heaven is the word of God, and it is wisdom who says come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you.

debates.question: Was the child really dead, given the saying that she only sleeps?

sides.position: It matters little — the touch of his hand and the power of his voice restored her, and the calling aloud was to show that she rose in answer to it
She was dead, and the hired mourners prove it, since they were not called until the death had been ascertained

debates.question: Why was food commanded for her at once?

sides.position: Because she was raised by a miracle but not to be preserved by one: God will do nothing by sovereign power that his ordinary providence can effect
Because the feeding is itself the figure — wisdom takes the hand and commands that bread be given, and the bread of heaven is the word of God

outliers.note: Alone builds the doctrine of grace out of the command to feed her, arguing that God provides food but does not eat for us, and provides salvation but neither repents nor believes for any man.
Alone turns the hired mourners into evidence for the death and then rebukes the custom itself, since those whose duty was to allay grief were eager to heighten it by fresh excitements.
Alone takes the return of the girl's spirit as proof that the soul is immortal and exists in a separate state, while refusing as needless the question where it had been.

themes: While he yet spake, there cometh one from the ruler of the synagogue’s house, saying to him, Thy daughter is dead; trouble not the Master.
But when Jesus heard it, he answered him, saying, Fear not: believe only, and she shall be made whole.
And when he came into the house, he suffered no man to go in, save Peter, and James, and John, and the father and the mother of the maiden.
And all wept, and bewailed her: but he said, Weep not; she is not dead, but sleepeth.
And they laughed him to scorn, knowing that she was dead.
And he put them all out, and took her by the hand, and called, saying, Maid, arise.
And her spirit came again, and she arose straightway: and he commanded to give her meat.
And her parents were astonished: but he charged them that they should tell no man what was done.
